blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
In many countries with high-prevalence generalized HIV epidemics, women continue to acquire HIV during pregnancy and 
breastfeeding. Women who become infected during this time also risk transmitting HIV to their infants. Incident HIV 
infection during pregnancy and breastfeeding contributes to a significant proportion of infants with HIV in very high 
incidence settings, and is of public health relevance for antenatal services that seek to test and treat all women with HIV 
as part of programmes for prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). 
Several strategies for preventing HIV infe

summary.text: Introduces the technical brief by explaining that women in high-prevalence settings still acquire HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding, raising the risk of transmission to infants. It notes established prevention measures and proposes oral PrEP as a complement, then lists the brief's aims.

blocks.title: What is PrEP?
blocks.content:
PrEP is the use of daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or co-formulated TDF/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) to prevent 
HIV acquisition. PrEP has been shown to be effective in a wide range of HIV-negative populations.

summary.text: Defines PrEP as daily oral TDF or TDF/FTC taken to prevent HIV acquisition by HIV-negative people.

blocks.title: WHO recommendation on PrEP
blocks.content:
In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that oral PrEP containing TDF be offered as an additional 
prevention choice for people at substantial risk1 of HIV infection, as part of combination HIV prevention approaches (1). 
This recommendation was based on a systematic review and meta-analysis (2) of high-quality evidence on PrEP’s 
effectiveness from clinical trial research. WHO included this recommendation in its 2016 update of the consolidated 
guidelines on the use of ARV drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection (3). 
The 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines on the use of

summary.text: Outlines WHO's 2015 recommendation that oral TDF-containing PrEP be offered to people at substantial HIV risk and how the 2016 consolidated guidelines addressed its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It notes that the benefits of preventing maternal HIV and mother-to-child transmission were judged to outweigh potential risks of fetal and infant drug exposure.

blocks.title: Why offer PrEP to pregnant and breastfeeding women?
blocks.content:
Pregnant and breastfeeding women living in settings where HIV incidence is greater than three per 100 person–years, 
particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, often remain at substantial and increased risk of HIV acquisition during pregnancy and 
breastfeeding. Biological factors increase susceptibility, and social and behavioural factors may increase exposure to HIV 
infection (Figure 1). Pregnant and breastfeeding women who acquire HIV at this time have a greater risk of transmitting 
HIV to their infant than women who became infected with HIV before pregnancy. 
Figure 1. Women may be at increased

summary.text: Explains why pregnant and breastfeeding women in high-incidence settings face increased HIV risk, with a figure listing biological and behavioural factors. It also summarises WHO recommendations on antenatal HIV testing, retesting and partner testing as part of prevention.

blocks.title: PrEP safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding
blocks.content:
The 2016 WHO guidelines state that there is no safety-related rationale for disallowing or discontinuing PrEP use during 
pregnancy and breastfeeding for HIV-negative women who are receiving PrEP and remain at risk of HIV acquisition (1). The 
guidelines conclude that in such situations the benefits of preventing HIV acquisition in the mother, and the accompanying 
reduced risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission outweigh any potential risks of PrEP, including any risks of fetal and 
infant exposure to TDF and FTC in PrEP regimens. The results from a WHO systematic review conducted in late 201

summary.text: Reviews evidence on the safety of PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding, drawing on a 2016 WHO systematic review of TDF use in HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. It reports that few adverse pregnancy, birth or infant outcomes were linked to TDF, and discusses data on drug levels in breast milk and infant bone and renal effects. It concludes that PrEP can be used in pregnancy and breastfeeding and as part of safer conception.

blocks.title: Providing PrEP to women who would most benefit
blocks.content:
Although there is limited experience with the use of PrEP in antenatal and postnatal care services, it is an important new 
HIV prevention method to consider, particularly for high-burden settings where women remain at significant HIV risk. 
There are three scenarios for which PrEP may be considered among HIV-negative pregnant and breastfeeding women:
1.	 a woman taking PrEP who subsequently becomes pregnant and remains at substantial risk of HIV infection;
2.	 a pregnant or breastfeeding HIV-negative woman living in a setting with high HIV incidence who is at substantial risk 
of HIV acquisit

summary.text: Describes three situations in which HIV-negative pregnant or breastfeeding women may be offered PrEP, together with testing, adherence counselling, monitoring and other prevention options.

blocks.title: PrEP as part of PMTCT in settings of high HIV incidence
blocks.content:
For high burden settings and for populations with high HIV incidence in low burden settings, all HIV-negative women 
should be offered prevention interventions at antenatal and postnatal visits (Box 1). In addition, PrEP could be offered as 
part of an enhanced comprehensive HIV prevention approach in selected sites where women experience ongoing high HIV 
incidence. Note that the other elements described in Box 1 should be considered for women in other antenatal and 
postnatal settings where PMTCT programmes are established but incidence does not warrant prioritization of PrEP.

summary.text: Describes how PrEP can be added to comprehensive HIV prevention in antenatal and postnatal care where HIV incidence is high, setting out eight elements of such a package in a box. The elements include repeat testing, partner testing and referral, condoms, STI screening and risk counselling. It also discusses risk assessment tools while cautioning that they should not be used to deny PrEP to women who request it.

blocks.title: PrEP for safer conception
blocks.content:
HIV-negative women in high prevalence settings remain at high HIV risk during 
the period of conception when their partners are of unknown status, or their 
partners are living with HIV and are either (a) not on ART or (b) are not virally 
suppressed (including partners recently starting ART, whose full viral 
suppression may take up to six months). Offering PrEP during this time could 
decrease the risk of viral transmission to the HIV-negative woman and reduce 
anxiety about HIV transmission at a time when couples are not always using 
condoms to prevent HIV transmission. The decision whethe

summary.text: Discusses offering PrEP for safer conception to HIV-negative women whose partners have unknown status or are not virally suppressed, stressing that the decision rests with the woman. A Kenyan risk assessment scoring tool for pregnant women is shown as an example.

blocks.title: Monitoring PrEP use by pregnant and breastfeeding women
blocks.content:
Although the currently available data are reassuring regarding the safety of PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding, 
active surveillance of mother and infant outcomes during PrEP use in pregnancy and breastfeeding should be part of a 
PrEP programme. WHO currently recommends1 that the active surveillance of ARV drug toxicity during pregnancy and the 
breastfeeding period focus on three areas. These three areas should also be monitored during PrEP use. 
1.	 Maternal adverse outcomes: monitoring treatment-limiting toxicities associated with ART in pregnant women, 
particularly mortality;

summary.text: Sets out how mother and infant outcomes should be actively monitored when PrEP is used in pregnancy and breastfeeding, covering maternal toxicity, adverse birth outcomes and infant growth and development. It also suggests integrating PrEP indicators into existing drug toxicity surveillance and continuity of PrEP services.

PrEP can be started or continued during pregnancy and breastfeeding in women at substantial risk of HIV acquisition.
A range of interventions should be offered to HIV-negative women in pregnancy and breastfeeding to prevent and detect 
incident HIV. These include condom promotion, counselling to reduce risk, risk assessment, STI screening and treatment, 
partner testing and treatment, repeat HIV testing and PrEP for women at substantial risk of HIV infection.

blocks.title: Key messages
blocks.content:
•	 PrEP is safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The ARVs used for PrEP, TDF and TDF/FTC, are frequently used in 
combination with other ARVs for HIV treatment. The latest WHO systematic review suggests that there does not appear 
to be a safety-related rationale for disallowing or discontinuing PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding for HIV-
negative women who are at continuing risk of HIV acquisition.
•	 PrEP could be provided as part of a comprehensive package. PrEP is part of a package of combination HIV

summary.text: Lists key messages of the brief, including that PrEP is safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, should be part of a comprehensive prevention package, and depends on adherence. It also covers disclosure, changing periods of risk, compatibility with hormonal contraception and cost-effectiveness.
